hook.text: Most of the code you'll be asked about in an interview, you didn't write. A colleague wrote it, or a stranger did, or more and more often an assistant, in a few seconds. What's being tested is whether you can read it: what it does, what it assumes, and where it's wrong.

plan.text: Three questions, answered on one piece of code: eight lines an assistant wrote to merge overlapping intervals, with two tests of its own. Both pass.

bugs.text: Question one. What kinds of bugs do AI assistants characteristically introduce? Code that is almost right.

bugs-survey.text: In Stack Overflow's twenty twenty-five developer survey, sixty-six percent of respondents named AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite, as their top frustration. Forty-five percent said debugging AI-generated code takes longer than expected.

bugs-edge.text: The usual suspects start at the edges. Boundaries: an off-by-one, a less-than where less-than-or-equal belongs, the empty input, the exact edge of a window.

bugs-assume.text: Unstated assumptions: input assumed sorted, unique, never null, or plain ASCII.
bugs-assume.spoken: Unstated assumptions: input assumed sorted, unique, never null, or plain ask-ee.

bugs-api.text: Invented APIs: a method, a parameter or a whole package that doesn't exist, or a real function called with the wrong signature. An invented package name is also a supply-chain risk, because an attacker can register it.

bugs-errors.text: Swallowed errors: a broad except that hides the failure the caller needed to see. And security: SQL built by string formatting, secrets pasted into the code, a missing authorization check.
bugs-errors.spoken: Swallowed errors: a broad except that hides the failure the caller needed to see. And security: sequel built by string formatting, secrets pasted into the code, a missing authorization check.

bugs-tests.text: Two more live in the diff around the code. Tests that agree with the bug assert what the code does, not what it should do, so they pass and prove nothing. And scope creep: renamed variables, reformatted files and unrelated edits, slipped in beside the change.

bugs-past.text: Notice which of them make a noise. An invented API fails as soon as its line runs, unless someone has registered the package. The other six run quietly and survive the happy path, so running the example proves very little. Three of them are in our diff.

debug.text: Question two. What happens in a code comprehension or debugging round? You're given unfamiliar code, often a few hundred lines, and told it's wrong, or slow. Where an assistant is allowed, the brief can be as plain as read, debug and optimize an existing codebase.

debug-report.text: Ours is eight lines, to fit the screen. The report: merging eight to ten, one to three and two to six returned one interval, from eight to six.

debug-read.text: Step one: read before you run. Find the entry point, the data flow, and the invariants the code relies on. This loop compares each interval only with the last one it merged, which is safe only if something about the order holds.

debug-repro.text: Step two: reproduce, with the smallest input that shows the failure, ideally as a test. Two intervals are enough. Three to four, then one to two, comes back as three to two.

debug-trace.text: Step three: form a hypothesis, and test it. Print the state where it might first go wrong, here after each interval, rather than change code and hope. After the first, it's right. After the second, it's wrong: one to two starts before the interval it was compared with.

debug-hypo.text: So the hypothesis: the loop assumes its input is sorted. Sort the input before the call, and the reproduction passes.

debug-symptom.text: Step four: fix the cause, not the symptom. Patch the symptom, by dropping any interval that ends before it starts, and the report's three intervals come back as an empty list, with no error at all.

debug-cause.text: The cause is the missing sort. Sort inside the function, then rerun the reproduction and the existing tests. All of them pass.

debug-explain.text: Step five: explain what was wrong, why the fix is right, and what else might share the flaw. Here, the loop relied on sorted input that nothing guaranteed, and the fix guarantees it.

debug-ai.text: If the round allows an assistant, it's a fine tool for asking what a function does, or what could make it return an interval that ends before it starts. It's no substitute for step two.

debug-past.text: And what else shares the flaw? Start with the tests. The two old ones passed before the fix and after it, so neither ever tested the order. Keep the reproduction as a third.

review.text: Question three. How do you review code an assistant wrote? Like a pull request from a capable stranger.

review-list.text: Check that it does what was asked, and nothing else. That every import, function and parameter it uses exists. That it handles the boundaries and the error paths. That it doesn't add an accidental O of n squared loop, or an N plus one query, one database call per row. And that its tests would fail without the change. Then run it.

review-diff.text: Go back to the diff as it arrived, before it shipped. It touches one function and its tests, and nothing else. It calls nothing that doesn't exist. It makes one pass over the input. So far, so good.

review-edges.text: The boundaries are where it breaks. Besides the missing sort, the comparison is a strict less-than. These are closed intervals, so one to two and two to three share the point two, and should merge. The code keeps them apart.

review-contain.text: And a merge sets the end to the new interval's end, even when that's smaller. One to ten, then two to three, becomes one to three. The merge shrank the interval it should have kept.

review-tests.text: Last check: its tests. Would they fail if the code were wrong? The first passes on this code and on a correct version alike, so it can't tell them apart. The second asserts that one to two and two to three stay apart. That's the bug, written down as a requirement, and on correct code it fails.

review-fix.text: Three changes fix it: sort the input, compare with less-than-or-equal, and keep the larger end. Then write the tests the review wanted: unsorted, touching and contained. On the assistant's code, all three fail, which is what failing without the change looks like. On the fix, all three pass.

review-where.text: Each bug is a boundary or an unstated assumption, which is where to look first. The obvious test touched none of them.

review-past.text: Then expect the follow-up: should touching intervals merge at all? Half-open booking slots, nine to ten and ten to eleven, don't overlap. So ask whether the end is inclusive, and write the answer down as a test.

next.text: The fix also added a sort, which takes the merge from one pass to n log n. Reading code includes judging what it costs. Next: algorithms as reasoning.
